properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Wish #37 from the dev_storyflow agent, 2026-09-07 (peer feedback line 7294), in their words: "when a field is rejected, say whether it MOVED (to another tool) or was REMOVED."

THE EVIDENCE IS IN THE SAME BREATH AS THE WISH, which is what makes it worth recording. They wrote "add_epoch lost `description` (it had one before?)" — and it never had one. The question mark is the whole finding: a bare refusal leaves a caller unable to tell a regression from a field that was never offered, so they guess, and a wrong guess about history is now in a field report. A third state is therefore needed beside their two: NEVER OFFERED.

OPTIONS, unranked, with what is cheap or expensive about each:
(a) A static table of renames and removals, consulted on refusal. Cheap to add, and it decays the moment somebody moves a field without updating it — a stale map that speaks confidently is worse than no map.
(b) Derive it from the toolsnaps. The goldens in tools/toolsnaps/ already record the served surface at every release, so "was this name ever offered by this tool, and does another tool offer it now?" is answerable from data the build already keeps, and cannot drift from the surface it describes. More work, and it needs the snaps shipped with the binary or embedded in it.
(c) Answer only the cheap half: on refusal, say whether ANY tool currently accepts that name, and which. This needs no history at all, and it covers the case that actually costs a round trip — the caller wants to know where to put the value, not what happened in v0.3.
(d) Do nothing; the refusal already lists the legal fields.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT, honestly: (b) is a history feature, and the reporter's real cost was a round trip, not a mystery. (c) may be the whole value at a fraction of the cost. Against that, the "(it had one before?)" question mark is a small false belief that entered a permanent record, and only the history half would have prevented it.
properties.name: OPEN — when a tool rejects a field, should the refusal say whether it MOVED to another tool, was REMOVED, or was never offered at all?
properties.rationale: Turned over rather than acted on because the three options differ by an order of magnitude in cost and it is not yet clear which half of the wish carries the value: knowing where a field went now, or knowing whether it was ever there. The distinction matters beyond this wish, because the same refusal is what would have told the reporter that DesignEpoch.description and Requirement.priority were never offered rather than removed — see fact:defect-a-declared-property-can-be-unreachable-and-invisible-to-the-reach-instrument-when-a-default-populates-it, which is the defect this wish sits beside.
